content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces Global Co-occurrence, an auxiliary pre-training objective for (masked) language models. Taking inspiration from GloVe, in addition to the MLM objective, a model is also trained to predict cooccurence counts (over the entire corpus) of the masked token with its nearby context words.

The authors’ main experiments are in the multilingual setting and over a variety of model architectures. They show consistent improvements in cross-lingual embedding similarity as well as downstream tasks such as unsupervised neural machine translation and cross-lingual classification and question answering. 

Overall, the idea is convincing and the results seem encouraging. However, the paper greatly suffers from its overall poor writing. This makes it hard to assess whether the setup for each experiment is rigorous and also harms overall understanding. Significant improvements to the writing, clarifications on the setup and additional ablations would make this a much stronger paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
* The approach is interesting and seems to yield meaningful improvements across various model architectures
* Experiments are conducted on both the embedding representations themselves and downstream tasks

Cons:
* The writing is quite poor. The paper feels rushed, with some sentences completely unintelligible, numerous typos and syntax errors. This significantly harms understanding and makes it harder to trust the reliability of the experimental settings. The introduction in particular would benefit from a significant rewrite. I also do not understand Appendix E and the contribution it tries to make: I would suggest removing it or integrating it earlier in the paper. 
* The structure of the different sections would benefit from re-organization and tightening. For instance, the back and forth between the results and critical experimental setup between the main text and appendix is tiring, especially since there is significant text duplication. 
* In the experimental setup, it is critical to identify the pre-training corpora, languages and vocabulary sizes used for each result. Training with fewer languages can lead to improved results on languages with large corpora due to a better vocabulary and more capacity. This is particularly true when comparing models with varying numbers of different scripts which can use a significant part of the vocabulary.
  * This is well done in Table 1 with the reimplementation of XLM on two languages. I would suggest adding vocabulary size and # of languages columns to the table to make it clearer that row 4 is the main comparison point to rows 5, 6 and 7.
  * This is less clear in Tables 2, 3 and 4 and 5. The appendix attempts to clarify the setup but it remains hard to parse. It would be clearer if experiments with the same corpora/vocabulary size/# languages were grouped together or highlighted and those columns were added. 
* The experiment in Table 2 is based on a single sentence and is very anecdotal. I would suggest moving it to the appendix to bring some of the aforementioned setup information back into the main paper. 
* Some more ablations would be welcome. A concern is that the improvements demonstrated in this paper are over baselines that are not state-of-the-art, and thus most of the improvement might disappear when comparing with those stronger baselines. For instance, whole-word masking / span-masking instead of MLM, using TLM pretraining in XNLI as done in Conneau et al, (2019), etc.
  * Have you tried using language-specific co-occurence counts for your GC objective? It would yield an interesting analysis on the importance of cross-lingual alignment.
  * Whole-word masking / span-masking are also partially motivated by the same goals. Do you still observe gains when applying GC to that setting? 
  * Are your performance improvements in XNLI orthogonal to those brought by Translation Language Modelling? I.e do you observe additional gains when using the auxiliary GC objective?
* The GC objective seems to be detrimental to NE-EN performance in Table 3, could you comment on that?



For illustration purposes and to substantiate my concerns on writing:
* Unintelligible sentences:  “Most importantly, n-co-occurrence information of different languages representing linguistic structures potentially overlaps each other in the isomorphic space for multilinguality as Zipf’s law may hold for n-co-occurrence and part-of-speech across languages.”
* Syntax / typos: 
abstract: refine different language spaces to overlap each other for forming isomorphic spaces -> to form 
abstract: The result is MLM-GC pre-training that the model learns local bidirectional -> where the model learns / rephrase. 
abstract: use “one” instead of 1
Intro: “For instantiation, MLM-GC pre-training is studied on multilingual corpora for multilingual tasks.” Instantiation is not the right word here.
‘to prevent the dot products get large”
“on on” p6
corpra p7
* Citations: format p6 “As reported in Google’s multilingual translation Johnson et al. (2017)”, no need to cite at every reference (e.g: SQuAD). 
* Appendix C.2 has a lot of repetition of what is also in the main text.
* Not clear what the role of appendix E is meant to be
* Intro needs significant rework
* Related work would be more helpful if presented earlier and more integrated with the intro.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity is by far the biggest issue, as highlighted in the prior weaknesses section. This makes the paper very hard to parse and also casts doubt on quality. Indeed, for this paper, a reliable experimental setup is critical and this is not easy to validate.
* Novelty seems to be a lesser concern. Though only one idea is introduced and based on prior ideas, it differs from the many other approaches to improve the MLM that have sought to modify which parts of the sentence were masked.
* Reproducibility is also a lesser concern. The idea is straightforward enough that its reimplementation is simple. Experimental details are given, though not always 100% clear. Code is already provided, though the README.md would also benefit from a significant overhaul.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduces a new auxiliary loss for MLM models, whereby models must predict co-occurence counts of masked tokens with their nearby context. The authors test this approach on several model architectures and mainly on multi-lingual settings. Their method seems to achieve good results. However, the paper is plagued by its poor writing, lack of clarity and insufficient clarity on the experimental setup. There is also a lack of ablations and the comparisons are to baselines that do not integrate the latest advances.

content.title: Thanks for your feedback and suggestion.
content.comment:
## W #1 
We have reorganized the paper and rewritten Introduction and Related Work.  We hope we can alleviate your major concern.

---

## W #2
Following suggestions, we highlighted the experimental setup in all tables by adding keywords, e.g., 12-layer Transformer encoder, 80K BPE, and Wikipedia dumps in 15 languages. 

---

## W #3
* Our previous reimplementation of XLM+PMI-masking is added to Table 4 and 5. However, we have a minor concern. PMI-masking is not a multilingual model. Without some explicit mechanisms, co-occurrence information cannot explicitly allow for cross-lingual representations. So we do not observe very strong performance. 

* Our method outperforms span-based methods: XLM + PMI-masking (Table 4) and MASS (Table 3) ( and ALBERT in Table 6). MLM-GC pre-training uses co-occurrence information for better context understanding and cross-lingual transfer. In contrast, span-based masking leverages co-occurrence information for context understanding but performs worse for cross-lingual transfer because of the lack of a mechanism to interpret cross-lingual supervision from co-occurrence information. 

* Yes, we have XLM+TLM+MLM-GC and observe additional gains. It indicates that the co-occurrence information gives extra supervision beyond a limited amount of parallel sentences. 

* With the objective of  $L_{GC}$, the model will associate  $H_{M_t}^TO_{w_{t \pm n}}$ with $H_{M_{\tilde{t}}}^TO_{W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$ of different languages if $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$, where co-occurred words  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and  co-occurred words $W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$ are parallel in different languages. In this way, MLM-GC underlies the basic assumption that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts (normalized by  $c_{lang}$), i.e.,  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and $ W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$  are parallel $\implies$ $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$. In sec 3.3  (new for rebuttal revision), we show that parallel pairs, e.g., "ist die" (De) and "is the" (En),  we show that, given the parallel pair "ist die" (De) and "is the" (En), the relevant pair "ist die" and "is a" (En), the irrelevant pair "ist die" and "locally known" (En), |log(ist die) - log(is the)| = 0.67 < |log(ist die) - log(is a)| =1.73 < |log(ist die) - log(locally known)|= 5.45 <  |log(ist die) - log(En avg)|= 5.58, where log(En avg) is the avg of En co-occurrence counts. For all the parallel pairs, the absolute difference avg is not 0, i.e.,  exact match for any pair. However, it still gives weak (not 0) but stable (relatively small with high confidence) supervision for cross-lingual transfer and confirms that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar (but not identical) co-occurrence counts. So it can be used in many models. 

* **The new section (sec 3.3 and Figure 2) provides deep analyses and ablation studies.** Our dev experiment (Table 1) shows n=2 is shows the best performance. We may explain that in our comparison of co-occurrence counts (Figure 2), $n=2$ has slightly smaller absolute difference $avg$ and the ratio $avg$ and narrower confidence (95\%) intervals in large-count bins ($>log(1e7)$) contributing to over 45\% co-occurrence counts on the multilingual corpora. 

* The clustering phenomenon can be interpreted from $L{GC} $.

* Unfortunately, we do not experiment with language-specific co-occurrence counts. If we understand this interesting question correctly, we think language-specific co-occurrence counts can also help cross-lingual transfer. Most of the co-occurred works are language-specific. The main difference is the shared pairs. For shared pairs, the absolute difference (|log-log|) is a constant 0, which gives very strong supervision for cross-lingual transfer. So we think language-specific co-occurrence counts work but underperform global co-occurrence counts.

---

## W #4 low performance on $Ne \leftrightarrow En$ 
Ne and En are distance languages. Even with parallel sentences in pre-training, the result is still bad (FLORES tasks, [1] ).  XLM and MASS fail in this task. However, XLM + OURS and MASS + OURS work, which means co-occurrence information gives some level of cross-lingual supervision.  Including bridge languages between NE and EN in pre-training is very useful (mBART + 25 languages), but MLM-GC pre-training does not require bridge languages. 

XLM + OURS and MASS + OURS are also not very strong because translation tasks require sentence-level translation knowledge. The knowledge gap between co-occurrence information and parallel sentences for cross-lingual supervision is still observed. Meanwhile, this knowledge gap can be also observed in Table 4 (sec 5.3, new for this revision) by comparing XLM+OURS with XLM+TLM.  Intuitively, co-occurrence information gives higher order of frequencies than unigram but lower order than sentences in cross-lingual transfer.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes an additional training objective for multilingual masked LM with global co-occurrence information. Inspired by Glove, a log-bilinear regression model is added for the training to minimize the embedding inner product and log co-occurrence counts between nearby tokens. The proposed method is evaluated on various multilingual and cross-lingual tasks, and shown to bring benefits.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

It is an interesting direction to consider global statistics in the pre-training phase (in addition to the relatively local MLM objective), especially in the context of multilingual pre-training.

The proposed method seems to be effective in various different tasks.

Weakness:

My main concern is on the calculation of the bilinear term. One major difference between Glove and Bert embeddings is that the latter is contextualized, therefore, in Eq. (2)/(3), I think that the “Ht” already knows the surrounding tokens and it seems a little strange to me to further use it to predict them (although this is not exactly the same as the prediction in MLM since the target is not one-hot).

There are too few analyses or ablation studies to show why the proposed method helps. For example, probably one way to address my above concern is to perform analyses on how well the bilinear calculation captures the global statistics.

Some of the results seem close and might need significant tests to show the stability. Moreover, in some of the tables (for example, Table 4/5), there seems to be no re-implemented baseline results? This might still be needed to directly show the benefits.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There are various places where the paper could improve for better presentation. For example, Fig. 1 could be adjusted for easier reading, Fig. 2 might need more explanations of what each points/clusters stand for.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes a global co-occurrence based training objective for multilingual LM, and evaluated its effectiveness on various NLP tasks. Nevertheless, I still have some doubts on the objective and think it might need more analyses and ablation studies to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

content.comment:
## W#1
Yes, representations are contextualized. But it has limitations. Span-based masking or PMI-masking finds the model considers easier multi-tokens instead of usefully hard context, where easier multi-tokens are in a subset of the context and result in sub-optimization. For instance, if a word splits into 2 sub-tokens in the context, the model may pay more attention to the 2 split sub-tokens instead of the context. They create spans across several tokens for masking to alleviate this pain. By contrast, we refine and regularize the final contextualized representations from global co-occurrence information across the context.

Moreover, co-occurrence information can improve cross-lingual transfer (our goal).

---

## W#2 

We will copy texts for quick review.

* With the objective of  $L_{GC}$, the model will associate  $H_{M_t}^TO_{w_{t \pm n}}$ with $H_{M_{\tilde{t}}}^TO_{W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$ of different languages if $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$, where co-occurred words  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and  co-occurred words $W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$ are parallel in different languages. In this way, MLM-GC underlies the basic assumption that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts (normalized by  $c_{lang}$), i.e.,  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and $ W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$  are parallel $\implies$ $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$. Although Zipf's law supports this assumption in linguistics, we are still interested in the question: \textit{how it reflects on the multilingual corpora we use.} To answer this question, we extract all (1100k) the pairs of parallel co-occurred words in $En$ and $De$ from the open-source translation tables (ORPUS, Wikipedia v1.0)$\diamond$, e.g., "ist die" ($De$) and "is the" ($En$), and compute co-occurrence counts on $\{De, En\}$ Wikipedia dumps (the same dataset we use in our experiment of the Cross-lingual Embedding task). For any pair, we compute the absolute difference  $| log(De) - log(En) |$, the sum $log(De) +log(En)$ (sorted into bins), and the ratio $| log(De) - log(En) | / (log(De) +log(En))$ for statistics in Figure 2. The figure tells us that the absolute difference $avg$ and the ratio $avg$ for all the pairs are relatively small and have narrow confidence (95\%) intervals. The absolute difference $avg$ is not $0$, i.e., exact match for any pair. However, it still gives weak (not $0$) but stable (relatively small with high confidence) supervision for cross-lingual transfer and confirms that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar (but not identical) co-occurrence counts. Meanwhile, the model is encouraged to distinguish relevant information from irrelevant information and to discriminate between the two relevant information across languages from co-occurrence counts and refine contextualized representations accordingly, which is beneficial for cross-lingual transfer. For example, in our experiment ($n=2$), given the parallel pair "ist die" ($De$) and "is the" ($En$), the relevant pair "ist die" and "is a" ($En$), the irrelevant pair "ist die" and "locally known" ($En$), we find $|log(ist\ die) - log(is\ the)| = 0.67 < |log(ist\ die) - log(is\ a)| =1.73 < |log(ist\ die) - log(locally\ known)|= 5.45 <  |log(ist\ die) - log(En\ avg)|= 5.58$, where $log(En\ avg)$ is the $avg$ of $En$ co-occurrence counts.

* **The new section (sec 3.3 and Figure 2) provides deep analyses.** Our dev experiment (Table 1) shows n=2 is shows the best performance. We may explain that in our comparison of co-occurrence counts (Figure 2), n=2 has slightly smaller absolute difference $avg$ and the ratio $avg$ and narrower confidence (95%) intervals in large-count bins (>log(1e7)) contributing to over 45\% co-occurrence counts on the multilingual corpora. 
---

## W#3

The previous reimplementation of XLM+PMI-masking is added to Table 4 and 5.  MLM+TLM is added to Table 4 as baselines. 

Our method outperforms span-based methods: XLM + PMI-masking (Table 4) and MASS (Table 3) (ALBERT in Table 6). MLM-GC pre-training uses co-occurrence information for better context understanding and cross-lingual transfer. In contrast, span-based masking leverages co-occurrence information for context understanding but performs worse for cross-lingual transfer because of the lack of a mechanism to understand cross-lingual supervision. We also include XLM + TLM for comparison. In UNMT, our method outperforms dictionary-based methods. However, in this experiment, XLM + TLM using parallel sentences in pre-training outperforms MLM-GC, which indicates the knowledge gap between co-occurrence information and parallel sentences for cross-lingual supervision. Besides, when applying MLM-GC pre-training for XLM + TLM, we still observe improvement. Intuitively, it indicates that the co-occurrence information gives extra cross-lingual supervision beyond a limited amount of parallel sentences.

content.comment: Thanks for the reply and updates! I'm still feeling that the calculation of the co-occurrence loss seems slightly unnatural to me. If the goal is to match the co-occurrence statistics, why is masking needed here? For example, would it be possible to forward a sequence with no masking and include such losses for every position (as in Glove)? Will the task be too simple to learn useful things in this way or the masking is needed to connect different languages (since the mask symbol is shared)?

content.title: Thanks for your feedback.
content.comment:
For the three questions:

* Yes, masking is important. As mentioned in Introduction (p 4), the model is encouraged to local learn bidirectional information from MLM and the global co-occurrence information from the global log-bilinear regression. Local bidirectional information is essential for language-specific knowledge and (other) structural similarities across languages. However, as indicated in Figure 1 and Table 2, simply using masking can not satisfactorily find word analogies across languages, which is useful for cross-lingual transfer.

* Yes, it is possible. We have tried it. We found that without masking, the model cannot capture language knowledge well. The model can only capture word analogies, cross-lingual embedding, and co-occurrence information.


* Yes, the task is too easy. The model still needs to learn some (other) structural similarities from masking.

Meanwhile, we actually discuss these three questions in this paper. Maybe, it is not obvious. In sec 3.3 (just around Eq. 4) or Appendix E, we discuss our early experiments. In the early experiment, GC can converge very fast because it is very easy to learn. In this case, the model will collapse to GC and ignore MLM (i.e., only GC). Then, as reported in Table 8, the model fails. In this failure, we observe that the model show very high performance on Cross-lingual Embedding and Word Analogy Tasks but very low performance on other sentence-level tasks. (Also, as mentioned in the paper, solving this problem is very simple. Just use the warm-up step (default 8k) for the learning rate.). It might indicate that GC can help the model to search cross-lingual embeddings and analogies but fail to capture some basic sentence-level knowledge. So we use both MLM and GC. Our goal is very simple. We aim at using global co-occurrence information for cross-lingual transfer in multilingual MLM pre-training because global co-occurrence information is available to all methods. Following this intuition, we conduct some empirical studies and confirm the idea. Meanwhile, compared to other methods of fine-tuning representations with additional resources, e.g.,  translation tables and parallel corpora (Table 3,4,and 5), our method does not require any additional resources. So we think we can use it as a regularizer or an additional objective in pre-training. 

We hope these early experiments can support our answers and alleviate your concerns. And, we may make it more explicit in the next revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the usefulness of Global Co-occurrence information in language modeling by changing the MLM pretraining to MLM-GC pretraining. MLM-GC combines the original MLM loss and a log-bilinear regression loss. The experiment shows that MLM-GC is beneficial for cross-lingual transfer tasks, which require the model to capture the embedding analogies among different languages. Additional experiments on SQuAD with ALBERT also show that MLM-GC can improve monolingual tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The method is simple: instead of predicting the masked token, MLM-GC predicts the log of co-occurrence counts by regression.
- The method didn't increase too much on the computational cost. The additional co-occurrence matrix is only allocated on CPUs not GPUs.
- The method can be easily adapted to existing multilingual models like XLM, MASS.
- The method shows consistent improvements in a wide range of cross-lingual tasks.

Weaknesses:
- The connection between "co-occurrence information" and "multilingual LMs" is not so clear to me. Why training an LM with explicit co-occurrence information can help the model better align all the languages together for cross-lingual tasks? I agree that the co-occurrence information can be shared among different languages, so maybe the model can somehow learn some analogies between all the languages by looking at the co-occurrence information. However, the connection is not very straightforward to me. It is better for the authors to illustrate this part more. It would be great if the author can show some evidence/analysis to prove that co-occurrence information is crucial for multilingual alignment (not only from the performance of multilingual tasks).

Question:
- For MLM-GC, did you have two separated LM heads for MLM and GC? It seems that you use the same output layer for both tasks. But I think these two tasks are very different from each other. How can you share a single output layer for these two tasks?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality:
- The experiments cover a wide range of tasks, showing enough evidence on the effectiveness of the proposed method.
- Some of the tables in the paper are very small, I can barely see the numbers after printing out the pdf pages. I know the page limitation may be too tight, but there are better ways to save space than using a tiny font for the tables.

Clarity:
- The method+experiment part is very clear to me. However, for the introduction, I didn't get much about the motivation (as I said in Weaknesses)

Originality:
- The concept of regressing the co-occurrence count is not new [1], but incorporating it into MLM training and investigating the effects in the cross-lingual transfer is somehow a new idea.

[1] Pennington, J., Socher, R., & Manning, C. D. (2014, October). Glove: Global vectors for word representation. In Proceedings of the 2014 conference on empirical methods in natural language processing (EMNLP) (pp. 1532-1543).
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, this paper has a solid result in the experiment, while the presentation of the motivation of the proposed method needs to be further improved. The overall quality is borderline. I would recommend acceptance if the authors can further address the questions that I have.

## Question: It seems that you use the same output layer for both tasks.
Yes, we use the same output layer. In our model, given the masked position $ t $, the contextualized representation $H_t$ and the pre-softmax linear transformation $O \in R^{d \times V}$ ($O_t$ stands for the output vector of the token at $t$):

1. $L_{GC}$ minimizes the error between scores of the pre-softmax linear transformation of $t$'s neighbors $[t-n,...,t) \cup (t,..., t+n]$ and the matrix of global co-occurrence counts, where scores are $ H_tO_{[t-n,...,t) \cup (t,..., t+n]} $,  i.e., excluding position $t$.
2. $H_tO$ is the probability over the vocabulary for MLM, and for $t$, the score is $H_tO_t$.

 In this way,  $L_{GC}$ optimizes $ H_tO_{[t-n,...,t) \cup (t,..., t+n]} $ to co-occurrence counts, and MLM pushes $H_tO_t$ to the maximum value (argmax) of $H_tO$. So $L_{GC}$ and MLM do not constrain each other. (sec 3.2, Eq.2, and Eq. 3)

---

## v.s. GloVe
Yes, the concept is similar. But MLM-GC underlies the basic assumption that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts  (supported by our empirical study of Figure 2 and Zipf's law). We believe it is not just an extension on multilingual corpora.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a novel way of utilizing global co-occurrence information in terms of n-gram (1, 2, and 3) to improve MLM pre-training. Specifically, the paper introduces an additional log-bilinear regression model that computes the error between the model’s pre-softmax linear transformation scores and the matrix of global co-occurrence counts. The resulting loss is also added to the standard MLM loss. Their proposed MLM-GC pre-training method shows improvement over the standard MLM pre-training in different downstream tasks - four multilingual tasks and one monolingual task. An interesting claim is that the proposed MLM-GC pre-training strategy leads to the regularization of contextualized representations using global co-occurrence information.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. The paper is well-written and easy to understand.
2. The evaluation is done over a large number of tasks.

Weakness
1. Although the usefulness of co-occurrence information is clear, the justification for updating the MLM loss is unclear from Section 1.
a)	Specifically, the drawback of Whole Word Masking and PMI-Masking mentioned is hard to understand -``Although methods like Whole Word Masking (Devlin et al., 2019) and PMI-Masking (Levine et al., 2021) now exist to leverage this information, the question still remains as to how meaning is generated from these statistics, and how the resulting representations might be learned from that meaning''.
b)	Key details of the simple case study of Figure 1 (a) and (b) are missing - how are the words selected? What do you mean by “large attention weights”?
2. In Equation 4, MLM-loss is simply added to GC-loss without any form of scaling or normalization. Please add more details to clarify this possible issue. I did not find any experiments related to this point.
3. Details of baseline models are missing. The choice of baseline models is relatively weak in Tables 1, 4, and 5, as the baseline models do not have access to any global co-occurrence information. This brings into question the effectiveness of the proposed strategy of MLM-GC pre-training.
a)	Why Whole Word Masking or PMI Masking is not used as baseline models
b)	As mentioned in Section 5, “MLM-GC pre-training regularizes the contextualized representations H[M]t by using n-co-occurrence information”, please explain why a comparison with other baseline models that regularize the contextualized representations (like ELECTRA) are not used for baselines. This would significantly improve confidence in the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and easy to follow. However, the limitations of prior methods are not clearly justified in Introduction as well as with the choice of baseline models (why other strategies of using some form of co-occurrence information not used as baseline models)

The paper provides sufficient details of model training and experimental setup and is reproducible. The authors will also make the code openly available on GitHub.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is easy to understand, reproducible, and considers many evaluation tasks. However, the novelty of the paper's main contribution (the MLM-GC pre-training strategy) is questionable. It is unclear why prior works that use some form of global n-co-occurrence information, such as PMI masking or SpanBERT, are not included as baseline models for performance comparison. It is not easy to understand whether the performance improvement is due to the addition of global n-co-occurrence information in general or is it due to the proposed MLM-GC pre-training strategy.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Thanks for your feedback and suggestion
content.comment:
## W #1
1) Introduction is revised.   We have two main points for the justification. 1. how cross-lingual transfer might be improved from global co-occurrence information on multilingual corpora. 2. leveraging global co-occurrence information might help the model understand embedding analogies across languages and then improve cross-lingual transfer, given that: 1) it is a proven idea on monolingual corpora GloVe; 2) analogical co-occurred words across languages may have similar frequencies/counts  (normalized by $ c_{lang} $ (sec 3.2)) as indicated by Zipf's law (empirical study figure 2). 

2)  Figure 1 (a) and (b) are moved to Appendix B. Given the parallel sentences in the figure, which have similar linguistic structures, the model shows similar behavior in information processing. It tells us that the co-occurrence information is significant for the model and represents structural similarities.

---

## W #2
More discussions are added to sec 3.2. Some early experiments are added to Appendix E.

In sec 3.2, we add scaling $ \sqrt{d} $ and weight $ \frac{1}{2n} $ to make training stable (Eq.\), where $\sqrt{d}$ is inspired by scaled dot-product attention to prevent the dot products get large. They serve as hyperparameters for $ L_{GC} $. Meanwhile, we find $warm\ up$ of the learning rate is significant. Without $warm\ up$, $ \sqrt{d} $, or $ \frac{1}{2n}$, the model may collapse to $ L_{GC}$ because $ L_{GC}$ converges too fast. In this situation, the model ignores the objective of MLM. Then, the model can only learn co-occurrence information and does not learn the language knowledge.

Besides, we also somewhat normalize the co-occurrence counts, using $ c_{lang} $ (sec 3.2)

---

## W #3
The previous reimplementation of PMI-masking is added to Table 4 and  5. Yes. PMI-masking uses co-occurrence information, which seems a reasonable baseline. However, we have a minor concern. PMI-masking is not a multilingual model. Without some mechanisms, co-occurrence information cannot explicitly allow for cross-lingual transfer. So the performance is not very strong. 

Yes, methods for contextualized representations might be the baseline. However, to the best of my knowledge, they require parallel data. So we think it is not directly comparable. Nevertheless, MLM+TLM are added to Table 4. MLM+TLM  uses parallel sentences for cross-lingual supervision. Meanwhile, we applied MLM-GC pre-training to MLM+TLM and observed additional gains. It indicates that the co-occurrence information gives extra cross-lingual supervision beyond a limited amount of parallel sentences.

---
## v.s. n-gram or Span-based masking.
Our method outperforms span-based methods: XLM + PMI-masking (Table 4) and MASS (Table 3) (and ALBERT in Table 6). MLM-GC pre-training uses co-occurrence information for better context understanding and cross-lingual transfer. In contrast, span-based masking leverages co-occurrence information for context understanding but performs worse for cross-lingual transfer because of the lack of a mechanism to interpret cross-lingual supervision from co-occurrence information.

---
## Empirical study
* With the objective of  $L_{GC}$, the model will associate  $H_{M_t}^TO_{w_{t \pm n}}$ with $H_{M_{\tilde{t}}}^TO_{W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$ of different languages if $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$, where co-occurred words  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and  co-occurred words $W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$ are parallel in different languages. In this way, MLM-GC underlies the basic assumption that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts (normalized by  $c_{lang}$), i.e.,  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and $ W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$  are parallel $\implies$ $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$. In sec 3.3 (new for rebuttal revision), we show that, given the parallel pair "ist die" (De) and "is the" (En), the relevant pair "ist die" and "is a" (En), the irrelevant pair "ist die" and "locally known" (En), |log(ist die) - log(is the)| = 0.67 < |log(ist die) - log(is a)| =1.73 < |log(ist die) - log(locally known)|= 5.45 <  |log(ist die) - log(En avg)|= 5.58, where log(En avg) is the avg of En co-occurrence counts.  For all the parallel pairs, the absolute difference avg is not 0, i.e.,  exact match for any pair. However, it still gives weak (not 0) but stable (relatively small with high confidence) supervision for cross-lingual transfer and confirms that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts. 

* **The new section (sec 3.3 and Figure 2) provides deep analyses.** Our dev experiment (Table 1) shows n=2 is shows the best performance. We may explain that in our comparison of co-occurrence counts (Figure 2), n=2 has slightly smaller absolute difference $avg$ and the ratio $avg$ and narrower confidence (95\%) intervals in large-count bins ($>log(1e7)$) contributing to over 45\% co-occurrence counts.

content.title: Common Questions and Key Points (1/2)
content.comment:
## Q #1: Justification and motivation?
We have two points as mentioned in Introduction.

1. n-gram or the co-occurrence information is the primary source of structural information available to all methods.  Some methods like Whole Word Masking leverage this information for improving context understanding in **monolingual** MLM pre-training. However, in **multilingual** MLM pre-training, the question still remains as to how meaning is generated from these statistics on multilingual corpora, how the structural similarities could be learned from that meaning across languages, and how cross-lingual transfer might be improved from that meaning.

2. leveraging global co-occurrence information might help the model understand embedding analogies across languages and then improve cross-lingual transfer on multilingual corpora, given that: 1) it is a proven idea to search embedding analogies on monolingual corpora (GloVe); 2) words and analogical co-occurred words across languages may have similar frequencies/counts as indicated by Zipf's law, which allows for better cross-lingual and multilingual representations.
	
---
## Q #2: How can co-occurrence information help the model better align all the languages together for cross-lingual tasks?

1.  Zipf’s law indicates that words or co-occurred words appear with different frequencies, and one may suggest similar meaning words or co-occurred words appear with relatively similar frequencies in other languages. 

2.  With the objective of  $L_{GC}$, the model will associate  $H_{M_t}^TO_{w_{t \pm n}}$ with $H_{M_{\tilde{t}}}^TO_{W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$ of different languages if $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$, where co-occurred words  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and  co-occurred words $W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$ are parallel in different languages. In this way, MLM-GC underlies the basic assumption that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts (normalized by  $c_{lang}$), i.e.,  $w_tw_{t \pm n}$ and $ W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}$  are parallel $\implies$ $X_{w_tw_{t \pm n}} = X_{W_{\tilde{t}}W_{\tilde{t} \pm n}}$.  In sec 3.3 Improved Cross-lingual Transfer and Figure 2 (new for rebuttal revision, see the figure for a quick review [link](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MLM-GC-F14F/statistics_gc.png) ), we show that parallel pairs, e.g., "ist die" (De) and "is the" (En),  from open-source translation tables, have similar counts/frequencies (normalized) allowing for cross-lingual transfer on multilingual corpora. For example, in our experiment, given the parallel pair "ist die" ($De$) and "is the" ($En$), the relevant pair "ist die" and "is a" ($En$), the irrelevant pair "ist die" and "locally known" ($En$), we find $|log(ist\ die) - log(is\ the)| = 0.67 < |log(ist\ die) - log(is\ a)| =1.73 < |log(ist\ die) - log(locally\ known)|= 5.45 <  |log(ist\ die) - log(En\ avg)|= 5.58$, where $log(En\ avg)$ is the $avg$ of $En$ co-occurrence counts. The model is encouraged to distinguish relevant information from irrelevant information and to discriminate between the two relevant information across languages from co-occurrence counts and refine contextualized representations accordingly, which is beneficial for cross-lingual transfer. For all the parallel pairs, the absolute difference avg is not 0, i.e., exact match for any pair. However, it still gives weak (not 0) but stable (relatively small with high confidence) supervision for cross-lingual transfer and confirms that analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar (but not identical) co-occurrence counts.



In conclusion, analogical co-occurred words across languages have similar co-occurrence counts/frequencies (normalized) allowing for cross-lingual transfer. 

---
## Q #3: Representations are already contextualized. Why do you additionally use co-occurrence information?

Yes, representations are contextualized. But it has limitations. Whole Word Masking (the new official implementation of BERT) (Devlin et al., 2019), SpanBERT (Joshi et al., 2020), and PMI-masking (Levine et al., 2021) find the model will consider easier multi-tokens instead of usefully hard context, where easier multi-tokens are in a subset of the context and result in sub-optimization.  For instance,  if a word splits into 2 sub-tokens in the context, the model may pay more attention to the 2 split sub-tokens instead of the context.  Whole Word masking, Span-based masking, and PMI-masking create spans across several tokens for masking to alleviate this pain. By contrast, we refine and regularize the final contextualized representations from global co-occurrence information across the context. 

Most importantly, co-occurrence information can improve cross-lingual transfer. Please refer to ##Q #2.

replying_to: Replying to Common Questions and Key Points (1/2)

content.title: Common Questions and Key Points (2/2)
content.comment:
## Q #4: Baseline and ablation studies for$L_{GC}$

* in Table 3,4, and, 5, we compare our model with baseline models, using the **same setup, configuration, and corpora**. We make it clear in tables for rebuttal revision.

* **v.s. SpanBert or Span-based masking** We compare our method with two span-based masking methods. In Table3, we observe substantial gains on MASS + OURS (and ALBERT in Appendix), where MASS (and ALBERT) is based on span masking. Span-based masking (also including Whole Word Masking and PMI-masking) implicitly leverages co-occurrence information for improving context understanding. In addition to the empirical study in Figure 2, the gain further confirms that MLM-GC pre-training significantly injects some signals for cross-lingual transfer beyond improving context understanding.

* **We have added our previous reimplementation of PMI-masking to Table 4 and  5 as baselines.** Yes. PMI-masking uses co-occurrence information, which seems a reasonable baseline. However, we have a minor concern. PMI-masking is not a multilingual model and is designed for masking. Without some explicit mechanisms, co-occurrence information cannot explicitly allow for cross-lingual representations. (MASS in Table 3 is better for comparison because it is an encoder-decoder model. But it is not suitable for Table 4 and 5.)

* We also added MLM+TLM to Table 4 as baselines. MLM+TLM  uses parallel sentences for cross-lingual supervision. Meanwhile, we applied MLM-GC pre-training to MLM+TLM and observed additional gains. It indicates that the co-occurrence information gives extra cross-lingual supervision beyond a limited amount of parallel sentences. (MLM+TLM is similar to models with  translation tables in Table 3.)

* **In Table 3, we compare our model with translation-based models.** These baselines are multilingual models for cross-lingual transfer with translation tables, co-occurrence information, and span-based masking (MASS). Our methods show strong performance.


Also, refer to ## Q #2. 

---

## Q #5: More deep analyses?

* **Our method outperforms span-based methods: XLM + PMI-masking (Table 4) and MASS in UNMT (Table 3) (and ALBERT in Table 6). ** MLM-GC pre-training uses co-occurrence information for better context understanding and cross-lingual transfer, whereas span-based masking leverages co-occurrence information for context understanding but performs worse for cross-lingual transfer because of the lack of a mechanism to understand cross-lingual supervision. **We also include XLM + TLM for comparison.** In UNMT, our method outperforms dictionary-based methods. However, in this experiment,  XLM + TLM using parallel sentences in pre-training outperforms MLM-GC, which indicates the knowledge gap between co-occurrence information and parallel sentences for cross-lingual supervision. Besides, when applying MLM-GC pre-training for XLM + TLM, we still observe improvement. We attribute the additional gains to the morphologies or the embedding space that is further refined by co-occurrence information to represent embeddings of similar meanings, e.g., embedding analogy. Intuitively, it indicates that the co-occurrence information gives extra cross-lingual supervision beyond a limited amount of parallel sentences.

* **The new section (sec 3.3 and Figure 2) provides deep analyses and ablation studies.** Our dev experiment (Table 1) shows n=2 is shows the best performance. We may explain that in our comparison of co-occurrence counts (Figure 2), $n=2$ has slightly smaller absolute difference $avg$ and the ratio $avg$ and narrower confidence (95\%) intervals in large-count bins ($>log(1e7)$) contributing to over 45% co-occurrence counts on the multilingual corpora.


* The clustering phenomenon can be interpreted from $L_{GC}$ that co-occurred words of similar co-occurrence counts are grouped.

---

## Q #6: Scaling, normalization, and hyperparamerters.

In sec 3.2, we add scaling $ \sqrt{d} $ and weight $ \frac{1}{2n} $ to make training stable (Eq.\), where $\sqrt{d}$ is inspired by scaled dot-product attention to prevent the dot products get large. They serve as hyperparameters for $ L_{GC} $. Meanwhile, we find $warm\ up$ of the learning rate is significant. Without $warm\ up$, $ \sqrt{d} $, or $ \frac{1}{2n}$, the model may collapse to $ L_{GC}$ because $ L_{GC}$ converges too fast. In this situation, the model ignores the objective of MLM. Then, the model can only learn co-occurrence information and does not learn the language knowledge. (the same as Common Question ## Q #5). 

We also somewhat normalize the co-occurrence counts, using $ c_{lang} $ (sec 3.2)

In addition, we add our early experiments in Appendix E to discuss these hyperparamerters.
